learningObjectives.title: Romantic style and composers (Chopin, Schubert, Tchaikovsky)

questions.q: What was Frederic Chopin's nationality?
questions.explain: Chopin was a Polish composer whose music was strongly influenced by Polish folk dances.

questions.q: Chopin composed almost all of his music for which instrument?
questions.explain: Chopin was a piano virtuoso and wrote nocturnes, waltzes, studies and dances almost exclusively for solo piano.

questions.q: Franz Schubert, famous for his songs, came from which country?
questions.explain: Schubert was an Austrian composer celebrated above all for his German art songs (Lieder).

questions.q: Which country was the composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky from?
questions.explain: Tchaikovsky was a Russian Romantic composer known for his ballets and symphonies.

questions.q: Which of these is a famous ballet by Tchaikovsky?
questions.explain: Tchaikovsky composed the ballets Swan Lake, The Nutcracker and The Sleeping Beauty.

questions.q: In Romantic piano music, what does the term 'rubato' mean?
options: Flexible, expressive stretching and relaxing of the tempo
Repeating a phrase an octave higher
Plucking the strings inside the piano
questions.explain: Rubato is the expressive give-and-take of tempo used by Romantic performers such as Chopin.

questions.q: A 'nocturne', a genre associated with Chopin, is best described as which of the following?
options: A lyrical, reflective piece evoking the night
A fast dance in triple time
A large work for choir and orchestra
A study designed purely for technical exercise
questions.explain: A nocturne is a slow, songlike piano piece with an expressive melody suggesting a night-time mood.

questions.q: Why did Chopin write many mazurkas and polonaises?
options: They were Polish dances that expressed his national identity
They were required by the Cambridge syllabus
They were the only forms allowed in the Romantic period
They were traditional Russian court dances
questions.explain: The mazurka and polonaise are Polish dances, and Chopin used them to reflect his patriotism and nationalism.

questions.q: What is a 'Lied' (plural 'Lieder')?
options: A German art song for solo voice and piano
A piece for solo unaccompanied violin
questions.explain: A Lied is a German Romantic art song, typically setting a poem for one singer accompanied by piano.

questions.q: Schubert's famous song 'Erlkonig' sets a dramatic poem by which writer?
questions.explain: 'Erlkonig' (The Erl-King) is Schubert's setting of a ballad poem by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

questions.q: What is a 'song cycle', such as Schubert's Winterreise?
options: A set of songs linked by a common theme or story
A single song repeated many times
A song sung in a round by several voices
A piece for orchestra with no singing
questions.explain: A song cycle is a group of Lieder connected by a narrative or unifying idea and intended to be performed together.

questions.q: What is 'programme music'?
options: Instrumental music that tells a story or depicts a scene or idea
Music printed in a concert programme
Music written only for the piano
Music with words sung by a choir
questions.explain: Programme music is instrumental music with an extra-musical narrative, image or idea, unlike abstract 'absolute' music.

questions.q: A Romantic orchestral work is given the title 'A Storm at Sea' and musically imitates crashing waves and wind. This is an example of what?
questions.explain: Because it uses instruments to depict a specific scene, this is programme music.

questions.q: In a Lied such as 'Erlkonig', what is the main role of the piano accompaniment?
options: To help paint the mood and imagery of the poem's words
To play a completely unrelated melody
To keep silent while the singer performs
To replace the singer's melody entirely
questions.explain: The piano supports and illustrates the text, a technique known as word painting, heightening the song's expression.

questions.q: Compared with the Classical orchestra, how did the Romantic orchestra generally change?
options: It became much larger with more brass, woodwind and percussion
It became smaller with only strings
It stayed exactly the same size
questions.explain: Romantic composers expanded the orchestra, adding instruments to achieve a wider range of colour and volume.

questions.q: What is 'chromaticism', a common feature of Romantic harmony?
options: The use of notes outside the main key, including many sharps and flats
Playing only the notes of a major scale
Keeping strictly to one chord throughout
questions.explain: Chromaticism uses notes foreign to the key to create richer, more expressive and colourful harmony.

questions.q: Which technical development allowed brass instruments to play a fuller range of notes in the Romantic orchestra?
options: The invention of the electric amplifier
The addition of strings to the trumpet
questions.explain: Valves gave brass instruments full chromatic capability, letting composers write more melodic and varied brass parts.

questions.q: Why did Romantic composers use a very wide range of dynamics, from ppp to fff?
options: To heighten emotional expression and contrast
Because they could not decide on one dynamic
To make the music quicker to perform
questions.explain: Extremes of dynamics were a key expressive device used to intensify the emotion central to Romantic music.

questions.q: The relentless galloping triplet figure in the piano part of Schubert's 'Erlkonig' is used to suggest what?
options: The horse riding through the night
questions.explain: The rapid repeated triplets depict the galloping horse, adding drama and urgency to the narrative.

questions.q: You hear a piece with a large brass section, lush chromatic harmony and dramatic swells from very quiet to very loud. From which period is it most likely?
questions.explain: An expanded orchestra, rich chromatic harmony and extreme dynamic contrasts are all hallmarks of Romantic music.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Music (0410) syllabus; Area of Study 3: Romantic Music
